story.logline: Your roof fills a tank with rain; summer rain is a trickle beside what your garden drinks, so how long until the tank runs dry and the tap takes over?

question: Will a rainwater tank keep my garden watered through summer?

source.title: Is a rainwater tank worth it for your garden?
quotes: A rainwater tank collects water from your roof so you can use it in the garden instead of tap water.
As a rule of thumb, every square metre of roof collects about one litre of water for every millimetre of rain, minus some loss to gutters and first-flush diverters, typically around 20%.
A 100 square metre roof in a place with 600 millimetres of rain a year can collect roughly 48,000 litres a year.
A typical garden in summer uses around 200 litres a day when watered by hand.
A small 2,000 litre tank fills and overflows in a single big storm and can be empty within ten dry days.
A 10,000 litre tank lasts most of a dry spell, but costs more and takes up space.
Many owners find a tank of 5,000 litres is a good middle ground for a small garden.
In most places it covers the wet months easily and runs dry in exactly the weeks you need it most.
Tanks also need a pump, cleaning, and in some areas a permit.

explain.caption: Summer is coming. Will your rain tank keep the garden green?
Gutters carry it into the tank, losing a little on the way.
Each summer day, your garden drinks from the tank.
But summer rain is a trickle beside what the garden drinks.
So the tank runs down, one dry day after another.
Once the tank is empty, your tap waters the garden again.
Your roof, your garden, your tank. Now make it yours.

simulate.prompt: Try your own tank, roof, rain and watering.

tradeoffs: A bigger tank lasts further into a dry spell, but costs more and takes up more space.
A small tank fills in one big storm, but the extra spills away and it can be empty within days.
Watering less stretches the tank, but some plants may struggle in the hottest weeks.
A tank saves tap water, but it needs a pump, cleaning, and in some areas a permit.
leftOut: Rain comes in storms, not as the steady daily trickle the model uses.
The model starts summer with a full tank; a dry spring would leave less in it.
Water that spills over the top in wet months is not shown.
The article gives no prices for tanks, pumps or tap water, so the model counts litres, not dollars.
Summer rainfall and the answer choices are assumptions; check rainfall records for your area.
Permit rules differ from place to place; check what applies to you.
